_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Shall we say he holds that an animal that expels a murky discharge [does not return and give birth] within its year: that is, within a year of its discharge. But the “within its year” above, in the dispute of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehoshua, means only within its year for giving birth, [the year] in which it was itself born, as I explained at the beginning of this section.
tosafot:a1.1: Shall we say he holds that an animal that expels a murky discharge does not return and give birth within its year: and all the more so this one, which gave birth to full offspring. And “within its year” is not precise; it means also a little after its year. For the kid was not born in that same year [as its daughters], since if so it would be tithed together with its daughters, and the first tanna does not count it. Rather, [it means] “in its year”: the day after its year. The Kuntres [Rashi] explained that this is like Rabbi Yishmael and goes further than Rabbi Yishmael, and he is right, since according to Rabbi Yishmael she does return and give birth on the first day of the second year, for he holds “from then on it is uncertain.” And the Kuntres asked: since it does not enter [the pen] with them, let us set the case where she was born in Nisan and gave birth in Elul, for then she could give birth again together with her daughters before the next Elul. But he was not precise in his wording, for just below we say that the first tanna accepts Ze’eiri’s statement; and the same applies, that an animal does not become pregnant less than thirty days after it was born. If so, it needs thirty days besides the five months of pregnancy, and he should have said that she was born on the twenty-fifth of Adar.
gershom:a1.1: Shall we say: from the fact that [the baraita] did not teach it so, “and let her give birth again,” but “and all her daughters gave birth to three,” conclude that he holds an animal that expels a discharge does not [return and give birth within its year]. The mother certainly [counts as having] expelled a discharge at the end of six months, when she gave birth, [for] thirty days, and could not give birth within her year but only in the second year; and the baraita implies that it speaks of [births] within their year.
gershom:a2.1: If you say that an animal that expels a discharge returns: that is, it does not remain in its discharge a full thirty days, [still] one that gave birth at the beginning of a year certainly does not return and give birth within its year. Therefore he must say “and all the daughters gave birth to three.”
rashi:a2.1: The difference between them is Ze’eiri’s statement: and the case is, for example, where the daughters expelled a discharge on the last day of the sixth month after their birth, and not on the first day of the seventh month. For now, when you allot thirty days for the discharge and five months of pregnancy, it turns out that they gave birth on the last day of their year, and they and their daughters enter the pen to be tithed, since they were born in one year.
gershom:a3.1: What is the difference between the first tanna and Rabbi Shimon: both agree that the old one [the original kid] is not tithed with them.
gershom:a6.1: And some explain that Rabbi Shimon, who said “I saw a kid that was tithed within its year,” holds that the kid and the daughters are all of one year and enter with them to be tithed. For example, the kid was born on the first of Elul, became pregnant after thirty days, and at the end of Shevat gave birth to three daughters; after thirty days, on the first of Nisan, those three daughters became pregnant, and at the end of Av each gave birth to two daughters. That makes six, and the three mothers, and the old one: ten, all of them of one year, and they are tithed within their year.
gershom:a7.1: And this is not reasonable. First, it is difficult for the one who asked “What is the difference between the first tanna and Rabbi Shimon?”, for we see that Rabbi Shimon requires the old one together with them and the first tanna does not. And further, the passage above, where they hold according to Rabbi Yehoshua, is difficult for me.
rashi:a3.1: And Rabbi Shimon does not accept Ze’eiri’s statement: that is why he says it was tithed within its year, that is, a day or two or ten days within the year in which they were born, for they did not wait to give birth until the last day of their year, even though they expelled a discharge at the end of six [months].
rashi:a3.2: Another explanation of “I saw a kid that was tithed within its year”: that is, within the same year in which it itself was born. How? After it was a month old it became pregnant and at the end of five months gave birth to three daughters; the daughters in turn became pregnant at the end of their first month and gave birth at the end of five months: that is a year. “Shall we say he holds that an animal that expels a discharge [does not return and give birth] within its year”: that is, within the year in which it itself was born, for its giving birth at the end of six [months] counts as a discharge, and therefore it does not give birth again until a month or two into the second year. And the first tanna too is speaking of a case where it was tithed within the year in which it was born, as Rabbi Shimon says, and below [the Gemara] explains what they disagree about. And this “within its year” they explain like the one above in the dispute of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehoshua, where we said at the beginning of this section that they disagree about an animal that expels a discharge, etc.
rashi:a3.3: The first tanna accepts Ze’eiri’s statement: there is no greater discharge than giving birth, and therefore she cannot give birth again within her year until after a day or two; and Rabbi Shimon, who did not go into this, holds that she can give birth again within her year, since he does not accept Ze’eiri’s statement. And now we can say that the first tanna holds that even an animal that gave birth returns and gives birth within its year, for this “within” they explain above, at the beginning of our chapter, as not literally within but at the end of a day or two. This version is not the main one, for there is a refutation for one who examines it closely: how can you find the daughters giving birth within their year? For example, where they conceived on the thirtieth day after their birth and gave birth five months later on the last day. If so, you can also find that she [the mother] gives birth again within her year.
tosafot:a3.1: In brief: Here too the Kuntres [Rashi] explained that her days of pregnancy are five full months, which seems to mean months of thirty days, and Tosafot say this is impossible. On the explanation that the dispute is about whether part of the day is like the whole, everything must be counted by the lunar year from the first of Elul to the next first of Elul, since the first of Elul is the new year for animal tithe, and the case works out only if the months of pregnancy follow the lunar months. For the first tanna, part of the day is not like the whole: a kid born on the first of Elul cannot receive a male until thirty full days after its birth (if Ze’eiri requires thirty days after a discharge, all the more so after its own birth); since Elul has twenty-nine days, that is the second of Tishrei; five months of pregnancy end on the second of Adar, when she gives birth; thirty full days later, on the third of Nisan, the daughters conceive, and they give birth on the third of Elul, in the next year. For Rabbi Shimon, part of the day is like the whole: the thirty days end on the first of Tishrei, she conceives then and gives birth on the last day of Shevat; the daughters’ thirty days end on the last day of Adar, which has twenty-nine days; they conceive then and give birth on the twenty-ninth of Av, within the year. One should not wonder that a small animal’s pregnancy follows lunar months: the Yerushalmi (Niddah, chapter 1) says that a donkey’s twelve months of pregnancy sometimes follow the solar year and sometimes the lunar year, citing the story of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Ashi, Rav and the donkey due to give birth, and the teaching “one that falls short does not fall short of the lunar days; one that adds does not add beyond the solar days.” It then cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that in the herds of Rabbi’s house some gave birth after incomplete months and some later, and resolves: one refers to an impure animal, the other to a pure one. It asks from “Do you know the time when the wild goats of the rock give birth … can you number the months that they fulfill?” (Job 39:1–2), which implies no birth after incomplete months, and answers that a pure wild animal is like an impure domestic animal and does not give birth after incomplete months, while a pure domestic animal does. Our sugya concerns a pure domestic animal. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a4.1: The first tanna accepts Ze’eiri’s statement: these three daughters expelled a discharge at the beginning of the seventh month after their birth, and the discharge lasted a full thirty days, and they cannot give birth within their year but only at the beginning of the second year. Therefore the first tanna did not say “within its year.”
gershom:a5.1: And Rabbi Shimon, who said “within its year,” certainly does not accept Ze’eiri’s statement; rather, they expelled a discharge for less than thirty [days] and gave birth within their year. And according to the first tanna she does not give birth after incomplete [months]; that is why he did not say “within its year.”
gershom:a8.1: Everyone says part of the day is like the whole: [so] they certainly give birth within their year.
gershom:b1.1: And they disagree about an animal lacking time, less than eight days old, whether it enters the pen to be tithed: according to the first tanna they do not enter; according to Rabbi Shimon they enter.
rashi:b1.1: And it is taught: as a support [not as a challenge].
gershom:b2.1: And it is taught: a support.
rashi:b1.2: And they are like: that is, in this matter it has the law of a firstborn.
rashi:b1.3: Just as a firstborn is consecrated before its time: for its sanctity is from the womb.
rashi:b1.4: So too a tithe is consecrated before its time: for an animal lacking time enters the pen.
tosafot:b1.1: So too one lacking time is consecrated before its time: and what is said in Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim (Temura 19b), “But what of one lacking time, which is not fit, and Rabbi Shimon said it is consecrated?”, refers to animal tithe, as is evident here, where Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis disagree about it; but with regard to other consecrated animals even Rabbi Shimon agrees.
gershom:b3.1: Just as a firstborn is consecrated before its time: at the moment it emerges from the womb.
gershom:b4.1: And is offered after its time: after eight days.
gershom:b5.1: So too one lacking time is consecrated before its time: in the tithe, and is offered after its time.
rashi:b2.1: Let one derive from consecrated animals: from peace offerings, which one cannot consecrate while they lack time, since sanctity does not take effect on them, as we say in Torat Kohanim: “And from the eighth day on it shall be accepted as an offering made by fire to the Lord” (Leviticus 22:27). I have only [that it is acceptable] as a fire-offering; from where [do we know] also to consecrate it? The verse states “as an offering.”
gershom:b6.1: Let one derive from consecrated animals: which are not consecrated until the eighth day.
rashi:b2.2: As [they share] redemption, blemish, substitute, eating: a firstborn and a tithe are not redeemed, for of the firstborn it says “you shall not redeem” (Numbers 18:17), and of the tithe “it shall not be redeemed” (Leviticus 27:33); but consecrated animals are redeemed when blemished. And these are consecrated with full sanctity even when blemished, which is not so of consecrated animals, as we say in the previous chapter (Bekhorot 14a): “All consecrated animals whose permanent blemish preceded their consecration,” etc., “except for the firstborn and the tithe.” And the substitute of a firstborn or a tithe is not offered, as it is written, “you shall not redeem; they are holy; you shall sprinkle their blood” (Numbers 18:17), and we say: they are offered, but their substitute is not offered, in Tractate Temura, chapter Elu Kodashim (Temura 21a); but the substitute of other consecrated animals is offered, as we say in the previous chapter (Bekhorot 14b): “Only your holy things”: these are the substitutes.
rashi:b2.3: Eating: a firstborn and a tithe are eaten in their blemish, the one by the [Israelite] owner and the other by a priest; but consecrated animals that became blemished are redeemed.
tosafot:b2.1: As [they share] redemption, blemish, etc.: it does not also say “and they are not brought from outside the Land [of Israel],” unlike other consecrated animals, because that is a matter of dispute there in the Gemara of Temura (21a).
tosafot:b2.2: Eating: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained that they are eaten in their blemish without redemption. This is somewhat difficult, since that is already included in “redemption.” It seems one should explain that their eating differs from that of other disqualified consecrated animals: they are not slaughtered in the market, sold in the market or weighed by the litra. This is by Torah law, as is implied in the first chapter of Temura (8a) and at the end of Ḥelek (Sanhedrin 112b) concerning the idolatrous city, where it excludes the firstborn and the tithe from “its animals”: [it includes] what is eaten in the manner of “your animals,” excluding the firstborn and the tithe, which are not eaten in the manner of “your animals.” For we learned: all disqualified consecrated animals are sold in the market, except for the firstborn and the tithe.
gershom:b7.1: As [they share] redemption, blemish, substitute, eating: a firstborn and a tithe are not redeemed, as it is written “But the firstborn of an ox … you shall not redeem” (Numbers 18:17), and of the tithe it is written “it shall not be redeemed” (Leviticus 27:33); but consecrated animals are redeemed. A firstborn and a tithe are consecrated even when blemished, as it is written of the tithe “good or bad” (Leviticus 27:33), and a firstborn born blemished is sacred; consecrated animals by law are consecrated only when unblemished. [Editor’s note in the printed edition: Our master’s words need explanation, since substitution does in truth apply to a firstborn and a tithe, except that the substitute is not offered and is eaten in its blemish by its owners. Perhaps it is a scribal error, and it should read: a firstborn and a tithe, their substitute is not offered; this is derived from what is written of the firstborn, “they are holy,” which we expound: they are offered, but their substitute is not; and for the tithe too we derive “passing” from the firstborn.] A firstborn and a tithe: [their] substitute [is not offered], for the firstborn derives “passing” from the tithe, and of the tithe it is written “he shall not exchange it” (Leviticus 27:33), and its substitute is not offered. Consecrated animals: their substitute is offered.
gershom:b8.1: A firstborn and a tithe are eaten by their owners in their blemish without redemption, but consecrated animals are eaten only after redemption.
rashi:b3.1: Regular, male, consecrated, gifts: tithe and consecrated animals apply to a regular [not firstborn] animal and need not be males; they must be consecrated by hand; they are not among the priestly gifts; and the tithe and peace offerings are eaten by their owners, as is explained in the chapter Ma’aser Behema (below, Bekhorot 56a), that the tithe is [like] a peace offering. But a firstborn is not regular, applies only to males, need not be consecrated, since it is sacred from the womb, and is one of the priestly gifts.
gershom:b9.1: As [they share] regular, male, consecrated, gifts: tithe and consecrated animals apply only to a regular [animal], and apply to males and females. Tithe and consecrated animals must be consecrated, which is not so of a firstborn. Tithe and consecrated animals of lesser sanctity are not a gift to the priest; [a firstborn] is a gift to the priest, as is taught in chapter HaZero’a [in Ḥullin]: twenty-four priestly gifts. And these [four points] stand against those.
rashi:b3.2: “Passing,” “passing”: “And you shall pass over to the Lord every one that opens the womb … the males” (Exodus 13:12); “whatever passes under the rod” (Leviticus 27:32).
tosafot:b3.1: He derives “passing,” “passing”: and even though one could also derive “under,” “under” (taḥat) from consecrated animals, as is said in the first chapter (above, Bekhorot 12a) concerning an animal that has some of the signs, here, with regard to consecration, it is more fitting to derive from “passing,” since “whatever passes under the rod” is a term of consecration.
gershom:b10.1: Rather, Rabbi Shimon derives “passing,” “passing”: just as a firstborn is consecrated while lacking time, so too is the tithe.
rashi:b4.1: The animal suppressed: its womb closed off and the fetus dissolved.
gershom:b11.1: The animal suppressed: when the animal closes off its womb and expels a discharge.
rashi:b4.2: Bubbles of blood: it expels bubbles of blood.
gershom:b12.1: Bubbles of blood: that it expels blood.
rashi:b4.3: To show it to a Sage: to know whether it was a fetus, so that it is exempt from the firstborn.
gershom:b13.1: To show it to a Sage: whether it is a full discharge or not.
rashi:b5.1: Forty days: for a woman who miscarries on the fortieth day must observe the days of impurity and purity [of a birth]; less than that, it is mere water.
rashi:b5.2: In an animal, how many: [how long] after it received a male must it wait until the discharge, for us to say it was an offspring and it is exempt from the firstborn?
gershom:b14.1: In an animal, how many: that is, when it miscarried, to know whether it was exempted from the firstborn.
rashi:b5.3: Isn’t this Ze’eiri’s: for it would have entered your mind that this is what he said: that thirty days is [the time] for the offspring to be formed, and on the thirty-first day it dissolves and comes out. (And this is what Ze’eiri says: a discharge holds back giving birth, since it does not conceive another offspring in less than thirty days.)
gershom:b15.1: There is no discharge in less than thirty days: and it implies that this is [the time of] the formation of the fetus.
rashi:b5.4: That was stated with regard to receptivity: from when it miscarried the first fetus, it does not receive a male for thirty days; but he did not speak of the days of the fetus’s formation.
gershom:b16.1: That of Ze’eiri was stated with regard to receptivity: once it begins to expel a discharge, it does not receive a male for thirty days; but in any case we do not know in how many [days the fetus] is formed. And some say: that was stated with regard to receiving, that before it receives the pregnancy it expels a discharge for thirty days; but the formation we do not know. (The note ends with an abbreviation, למ״ה.)
rashi:b6.1: We found one who purchases from a gentile: what his law is, as our mishna teaches.
gershom:b17.1: We found one who purchases from a gentile: [the mishna] has already ruled on the law of one who purchases an animal from a gentile.
rashi:b6.2: He would have boasted to him: the seller says, “Take it, for it has already borne a firstborn, and you will no longer need to give its offspring to the priest.”
tosafot:b6.1: He would have boasted to him: the Kuntres [Rashi] explained, that it has already borne a firstborn and will no longer be in danger in giving birth. [The Rashi printed on the daf says instead: you will no longer need to give its offspring to the priest.] But a gentile, even if he said so to him, there is no truth in his words. And one may learn from his explanation that a gentile, even when speaking innocently, is not believed, for he says so to make his merchandise more attractive. One may also explain that the “boasting” here is that it has already been exempted from the firstborn.
gershom:b18.1: He would have boasted to him: for he would say to him, “Know that it is one that has borne offspring,” and further, that it has already been exempted from the firstborn.
rashi:b7.1: Uncertain: and the reason the seller did not praise it for this is that he thought the buyer wanted it for slaughter.
gershom:b19.1: An uncertain firstborn: for the seller thinks this buyer wants it for slaughter, and therefore he does not praise it for having borne offspring; so there is concern that it gave birth, and it is an uncertain firstborn.
tosafot:b7.1: Rabbi Yoḥanan says: definitely non-sacred. Halakhot Gedolot rules in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan; and in Beitza (4b) we say that between Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan the halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan, and in the chapter Mi SheHotziuhu (Eiruvin 47b) we say that between Shmuel and Rabbi Yoḥanan the halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan.
gershom:b20.1: Since there is a prohibition: if an Israelite eats the firstborn.
gershom:b21.1: He would have notified him: “Know that it has not yet borne a firstborn.”
rashi:b8.1: If he did not inform him: on the four occasions in the year, a seller who sold a cow for slaughter and on the same day sold its offspring to another for slaughter must inform him, “I sold its mother for slaughter.” If he did not inform him, the buyer goes and slaughters the offspring and need not go back and ask whether its mother was slaughtered that day.
gershom:b22.1: If he did not inform him: as we learned, on four occasions in the year one who sells an animal to his fellow must inform him, “I sold its mother for slaughter,” etc. If he did not inform him, he slaughters and does not refrain, for if he had in fact sold its mother he would have informed him, because of the prohibition of “it and its offspring.”
gershom:b23.1: Shall we say this is a conclusive refutation of Rav and Shmuel: for from here we learn that it is definitely non-sacred.
rashi:b8.2: There, the Merciful One made it depend on the seller: for he must inform him, as we say in Sheḥitat Ḥullin (83b): “One day”: a special day, which requires an announcement; that is, the special day, the four occasions in the year set aside for this, when the seller must announce, “I sold its mother for slaughter.”
tosafot:b8.1: There, the matter depends on the seller: for the seller knows that the buyer is buying in order to slaughter, and he transgresses the prohibition of “before the blind” if he does not inform him; but the buyer had no need to consider that he might have sold its mother or its daughter.
gershom:b24.1: Rav and Shmuel could say to you: it is not comparable. There, why does he slaughter [without refraining]? Because the matter depends on the seller, to inform him.
rashi:b8.3: Here, the matter depends on the buyer: as it is written, “of your herd and of your flock” (Deuteronomy 15:19): the one to whom the animal belongs must set aside its firstborns.
tosafot:b8.2: Here, the matter depends on the buyer: for it is on him to investigate his animal, whether it is obligated in the firstborn.
gershom:b25.1: Here, the matter depends on the buyer, to ask him whether it is a firstborn or not; and since he did not ask him, it is therefore uncertain.
rashi:b9.1: Mishna. That must be buried: the mass [of blood], which is forbidden for benefit, since perhaps it was a male offspring that dissolved, and it was consecrated as a firstborn when it emerged.
tosafot:b9.1: A large animal that expelled a mass of blood must be buried: even though it is taught in the chapter Behema HaMakshah (Ḥullin 77a) that a first-bearing animal that miscarried a placenta, one throws it to the dogs, which is explained there as because we combine the minority [of fetuses] that are a shapeless form with the half that are females, here it is different, as the Gemara explains: in order to publicize that it was exempted from the firstborn. As for the Gemara’s reaching this only because of Rabbi Ḥiyya, who says, “Since it does not impart impurity, neither through contact nor through carrying, why must it be buried?”, and answering, “in order to publicize,” etc.: even without this, the reason of publicity would have been needed. Rather, given what Rabbi Ḥiyya said, it was not so comfortable that it be buried for the reason of publicity, since even if one knew that it had given birth to something sacred, it would not require burial, because they are nullified.
rashi:b10.1: Gemara. It does not impart impurity through contact or carrying: as a carcass does. Now it enters your mind [that this is] because we are not concerned that perhaps an offspring dissolved there; [if so,] why must it be buried?
gershom:b26.1: Why must it be buried? Since it does not impart impurity, evidently we are not concerned that it contains a full offspring. [The answer:] it must be buried in order to publicize that it was exempted from the firstborn.
